specStatements.text: Students should be able to explain how the structures of plant tissues are related to their functions.
Plant tissues include: epidermal tissues; palisade mesophyll; spongy mesophyll; xylem and phloem; meristem tissue found at the growing tips of shoots and roots.
The leaf is a plant organ. Knowledge limited to epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem, and guard cells surrounding stomata.
Students should be able to explain how the structure of root hair cells, xylem and phloem are adapted to their functions.
Students should be able to explain the effect of changing temperature, humidity, air movement and light intensity on the rate of transpiration.
Students should be able to understand and use simple compound measures such as the rate of transpiration.

Students should be able to: translate information between graphical and numerical form; plot and draw appropriate graphs, selecting appropriate scales for axes; extract and interpret information from graphs, charts and tables.
The roots, stem and leaves form a plant organ system for transport of substances around the plant.
Students should be able to describe the process of transpiration and translocation, including the structure and function of the stomata.
Root hair cells are adapted for the efficient uptake of water by osmosis, and mineral ions by active transport.

Xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves. It is composed of hollow tubes strengthened by lignin adapted for the transport of water in the transpiration stream.
The role of stomata and guard cells are to control gas exchange and water loss.
Phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage. The movement of food molecules through phloem tissue is called translocation.
Phloem is composed of tubes of elongated cells. Cell sap can move from one phloem cell to the next through pores in the end walls.
Detailed structure of phloem tissue or the mechanism of transport is not required.

scopeNotes.statement: Detailed structure of phloem tissue or the mechanism of transport is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Detailed structure of phloem tissue and the mechanism of transport are not required, so phloem is described only as tubes of elongated cells with pores in the end walls through which cell sap can move from one cell to the next. Sieve tube elements, sieve plates, companion cells and any pressure-flow or mass-flow explanation of how translocation is driven are deliberately absent, and no misconception or question asks what makes sugars move.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of the leaf is limited to epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem, and guard cells surrounding stomata.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Knowledge of the leaf is limited to the epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem, and guard cells surrounding stomata. Nothing beyond those named structures is introduced: the waxy cuticle, vascular bundle arrangement, chloroplast internal structure and the mechanism by which guard cells change shape are all left out, and the concepts, misconceptions and questions use only the listed tissues.

concepts.definition: The tissue that covers the outer surfaces of a plant. In a leaf it forms the upper and lower epidermis, a protective covering that contains the guard cells surrounding the stomata.
The leaf tissue lying just below the upper epidermis. Its closely packed cells contain many chloroplasts, so this is the main tissue in which photosynthesis takes place.
The leaf tissue lying below the palisade mesophyll. Its cells are loosely packed with air spaces between them, so gases can diffuse to and from the photosynthesising cells.
Plant tissue found at the growing tips of shoots and roots. Its cells divide to produce the new cells a plant needs for growth.

The tissue that transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves. It is composed of hollow tubes strengthened by lignin, adapted for the transport of water in the transpiration stream.

The tissue that transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage. It is composed of tubes of elongated cells, and cell sap can move from one phloem cell to the next through pores in the end walls.
The movement of food molecules, as dissolved sugars, through phloem tissue from the leaves to the rest of the plant.

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, which diffuses out of the leaves through the stomata. The transpiration stream is the movement of water taken up by the roots and carried up through the xylem to the stems and leaves that replaces it.
A cell on the outside of a root, drawn out into a long thin hair that gives a large surface area. It is adapted for the efficient uptake of water by osmosis and of mineral ions by active transport.
A stoma is a pore in the epidermis of a leaf. Each stoma is surrounded by a pair of guard cells that open and close it. The role of stomata and guard cells is to control gas exchange and water loss.
The roots, stem and leaves, which work together as an organ system for the transport of substances around the plant.

misconceptions.question: Which tissue transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant?
misconceptions.correct: Phloem tissue transports the dissolved sugars; xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves.
misconceptions.misconception: Xylem and phloem are both transport tubes carrying the same things, so xylem carries the sugars made in the leaves and phloem carries the water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two tissues are learned together and drawn side by side in the same diagram, so students remember that a plant moves water and food without separating which tissue does which job.
misconceptions.correction: Xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves. Phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage.

misconceptions.question: By which process do mineral ions enter a root hair cell from the soil?
misconceptions.correct: Mineral ions are taken up by active transport; only the water enters by osmosis.
misconceptions.misconception: Mineral ions are dissolved in the soil water, so they are swept into the root hair cell by osmosis along with that water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Water and mineral ions are absorbed at the same place and at the same time, and osmosis is the transport process students meet first, so it gets used for everything entering the root.
misconceptions.correction: Root hair cells are adapted for the efficient uptake of water by osmosis, and mineral ions by active transport. Osmosis moves water only.

misconceptions.question: What is a stoma and what is a guard cell?
misconceptions.correct: A stoma is a pore; the guard cells are the pair of cells surrounding it that open and close it.
misconceptions.misconception: The stomata are the cells in the leaf surface, and the guard cells are the holes in between that they are guarding.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name guard cell sounds like something standing around an opening rather than the opening itself, so the two labels get swapped when a diagram is read.
misconceptions.correction: Stomata are pores, with guard cells surrounding stomata. The role of stomata and guard cells is to control gas exchange and water loss.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the rate of transpiration when the air around a leaf becomes more humid?
misconceptions.misconception: Humid air is full of water, so more water moves out of the leaf and the rate of transpiration goes up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link the idea of more water in the air with more water moving, instead of comparing the water vapour inside the leaf with the water vapour in the air outside.
misconceptions.correction: Increasing humidity decreases the rate of transpiration, because water vapour diffuses out of the stomata more slowly when the air outside the leaf already holds a lot of water vapour.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the rate of transpiration when air movement across a leaf increases?
misconceptions.misconception: Moving air cools a leaf down, so less water evaporates from it and transpiration slows.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience of wind feeling cold is carried over to the leaf, and cooling is correctly linked with slower evaporation, so the wrong overall answer follows from a sensible-looking chain.
misconceptions.correction: Increasing air movement increases the rate of transpiration, because moving air carries water vapour away from around the stomata.

misconceptions.question: What is xylem tissue composed of?
misconceptions.misconception: Xylem is made of living cells joined end to end, with pores in the end walls that let cell sap pass from one cell to the next.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Xylem and phloem are taught in the same breath, so the feature that belongs to phloem, pores in the end walls of elongated cells, is attached to xylem instead.
misconceptions.correction: Xylem is composed of hollow tubes strengthened by lignin, adapted for the transport of water in the transpiration stream. It is phloem that is composed of tubes of elongated cells with pores in the end walls.

misconceptions.question: Which leaf tissue is the main site of photosynthesis, and which one contains the air spaces?
misconceptions.correct: Palisade mesophyll is the main photosynthetic tissue; spongy mesophyll contains the air spaces.
misconceptions.misconception: The spongy mesophyll does most of the photosynthesis because it fills most of the leaf, and the palisade layer is the one holding the air spaces.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two mesophyll names are easily swapped, and the spongy layer often looks larger in a leaf diagram, so students assume it must be doing the main job.
misconceptions.correction: Palisade mesophyll cells contain many chloroplasts and are the main photosynthetic tissue of the leaf. Spongy mesophyll cells are loosely packed with air spaces that let gases diffuse.

misconceptions.question: Is a leaf a tissue or an organ?
misconceptions.correct: A leaf is a plant organ.
misconceptions.misconception: A leaf is a tissue, because it is one thin flat part of the plant made of cells doing the same job.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word organ is associated with animals such as the heart or lungs, and a leaf looks like a single uniform sheet from the outside rather than a set of different tissues.
misconceptions.correction: The leaf is a plant organ. It is built from several tissues working together: epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem, and guard cells surrounding stomata.

misconceptions.question: Shoot A loses 3.0 cm3 of water in 60 minutes and shoot B loses 2.0 cm3 in 20 minutes. Which shoot has the higher rate of transpiration?
misconceptions.correct: Shoot B, at 0.10 cm3 per minute compared with 0.05 cm3 per minute for shoot A.
misconceptions.misconception: The shoot that has lost the largest volume of water has the highest rate of transpiration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students compare the numbers in the volume column directly, because the volume is the quantity that was measured and the time taken is recorded separately.
misconceptions.correction: The rate of transpiration is a compound measure: it is the volume of water lost divided by the time taken, for example in cm3 per minute, so the times must be taken into account before the shoots are compared.

mcqs.stem: What does xylem tissue transport, and in which direction?

options.text: Dissolved sugars, from the leaves to all parts
options.rationale: A student who treats xylem and phloem as interchangeable transport tubes picks the sugar route for xylem. It is wrong because transporting dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant is the function of phloem tissue.

options.text: Water and mineral ions, from the roots to leaves
options.rationale: Xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves, carrying the water in the transpiration stream.

options.text: Cell sap, from each living cell to the next one
options.rationale: A student who pictures xylem as living cells joined by pores in their end walls describes cell sap passing along. It is wrong because xylem is composed of hollow tubes strengthened by lignin; pores in end walls belong to phloem.

options.text: Mineral ions, drawn into the roots by osmosis
options.rationale: A student who believes mineral ions move by osmosis chooses the osmosis option. It is wrong because osmosis moves water only, mineral ions are taken up by active transport, and xylem carries both water and mineral ions upwards.

mcqs.stem: How does a root hair cell take up water and mineral ions from the soil?

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and ions by active transport
options.rationale: Root hair cells are adapted for the efficient uptake of water by osmosis, and mineral ions by active transport.

options.text: Water and mineral ions both enter the cell by osmosis
options.rationale: A student who believes dissolved mineral ions are swept in with the water uses osmosis for both. It is wrong because osmosis moves water only; mineral ions are taken up by active transport.

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and sugars by translocation
options.rationale: A student who confuses what each transport tissue carries thinks the root takes in sugars. It is wrong because translocation moves dissolved sugars from the leaves; roots take up water and mineral ions.

options.text: Water enters through pores in the cells' end walls
options.rationale: A student who thinks plant transport cells are joined by pores in their end walls applies that to the root. It is wrong because pores in end walls are a feature of phloem, and water enters a root hair cell by osmosis.

options.text: Water and mineral ions move up to the leaves
options.rationale: A student who swaps the roles of the two transport tissues gives the xylem job here. It is wrong because that movement is the transpiration stream in xylem, not translocation.

options.text: Dissolved sugars move to the rest of the plant
options.rationale: Translocation is the movement of food molecules through phloem tissue, carrying dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage.

options.text: Cell sap moves through tubes stiffened by lignin
options.rationale: A student who attaches lignified hollow tubes to the movement of cell sap picks this. It is wrong because lignin strengthens xylem; translocation happens in phloem tubes of elongated cells.

options.text: Water and mineral ions enter cells by osmosis
options.rationale: A student who explains all plant transport by osmosis picks the osmosis option. It is wrong because osmosis moves water only, and translocation is the movement of dissolved sugars in phloem.

mcqs.stem: What is the role of the guard cells that surround each stoma?

options.text: They control gas exchange and water loss from the leaf
options.rationale: The role of stomata and guard cells is to control gas exchange and water loss, the guard cells opening and closing each pore.

options.text: They are the pores through which gases pass in or out
options.rationale: A student who has swapped the two labels treats the guard cells as the holes. It is wrong because the stomata are the pores; guard cells are the cells surrounding them.

options.text: They open more widely as the surrounding air grows humid
options.rationale: A student who believes humid air speeds up water loss expects the guard cells to respond to humidity. It is wrong because the role of stomata and guard cells is to control gas exchange and water loss, and humidity slows transpiration rather than opening the pores.

options.text: They enclose air spaces where photosynthesis occurs
options.rationale: A student who thinks the air-space tissue is the main photosynthetic tissue attaches that role to the guard cells. It is wrong because air spaces are in the spongy mesophyll, and palisade mesophyll is the main photosynthetic tissue.

mcqs.stem: A potted plant is moved from a cool, shaded room with still, humid air into a warm, brightly lit room with moving, dry air. What happens to its rate of transpiration?

options.text: It decreases, since drier air holds less water vapour
options.rationale: A student who believes humid air drives more water out of a leaf expects drier air to slow transpiration. It is wrong because decreasing humidity increases the rate of transpiration.

options.text: It decreases, as the moving air cools the leaf surface
options.rationale: A student who believes moving air cools a leaf and so slows evaporation picks a decrease. It is wrong because increasing air movement carries water vapour away from the stomata and increases the rate of transpiration.

options.text: It stays the same, as the same volume of water was lost
options.rationale: A student who thinks of transpiration as a total volume rather than a rate sees no change. It is wrong because the rate is the volume of water lost per unit time, and these conditions make that rate higher.

options.text: It increases, as water evaporates and diffuses out faster
options.rationale: Higher temperature, higher light intensity, greater air movement and lower humidity each increase the rate of transpiration: the stomata open in the light and water vapour diffuses out of them more quickly.

mcqs.stem: A student measured the water lost by three identical shoots. Shoot A lost 1.2 cm3 in 60 minutes in still air at 20 degrees C. Shoot B lost 2.4 cm3 in 60 minutes in moving air at 20 degrees C. Shoot C lost 2.0 cm3 in 40 minutes in still air at 30 degrees C. Which conclusion do the results support?

options.text: The highest rate of water loss was in moving air at 20 C
options.rationale: A student who reads off the largest volume, 2.4 cm3, without dividing by the time picks shoot B. It is wrong because rate is volume per unit time, and shoot B's rate is 0.04 cm3 per minute.

options.text: The lowest rate of water loss was in moving air at 20 C
options.rationale: A student who believes moving air slows water loss expects the moving-air shoot to be lowest. It is wrong because shoot B lost water at 0.04 cm3 per minute against shoot A's 0.02, so air movement increased the rate.

options.text: The highest water-loss rate was in still air at 30 C
options.rationale: Rate of transpiration is volume divided by time: shoot C lost 2.0 cm3 in 40 minutes, which is 0.05 cm3 per minute, higher than shoot B at 0.04 and shoot A at 0.02.

options.text: Still air at 20 C gave the highest rate of water loss
options.rationale: A student who believes still, humid air increases water loss picks shoot A. It is wrong because shoot A had the lowest rate, 0.02 cm3 per minute, so still air gave the least transpiration.

mcqs.stem: How is the structure of palisade mesophyll related to its function in a leaf?

options.text: Its cells are spread apart to let gases move around
options.rationale: A student who swaps the two mesophyll tissues gives palisade the air spaces. It is wrong because the loosely packed cells with air spaces are the spongy mesophyll.

options.text: Its cells are living tubes with pores in the end walls
options.rationale: A student who pictures plant tissue as living cells joined by pores in their end walls, the m06 belief about xylem, applies that structure to palisade. It is wrong because pores in the end walls of elongated living cells are a feature of phloem; palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts to absorb light for photosynthesis.

options.text: Its cells hold many chloroplasts that absorb light
options.rationale: Palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface of the leaf, so the tissue is structured to absorb light for photosynthesis.

options.text: Its cells are one tissue that makes up the whole leaf
options.rationale: A student who believes a leaf is a single tissue rather than an organ makes palisade the whole leaf. It is wrong because the leaf is a plant organ built from several tissues, and this does not link structure to function.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the process of transpiration?

options.text: Sugars dissolve in cells and move down the xylem
options.rationale: A student who swaps the roles of xylem and phloem describes sugar movement in xylem. It is wrong because that is translocation in phloem, and transpiration is the loss of water vapour.

options.text: Water leaves through the guard cells acting as pores
options.rationale: A student who thinks the guard cells are the holes describes water leaving through them. It is wrong because the stomata are the pores and the guard cells surround and control them.

options.text: More water vapour diffuses out into the humid air
options.rationale: A student who believes humid air is full of water and so drives more water out of the leaf describes transpiration speeding up in humid air. It is wrong because increasing humidity actually slows transpiration, as water vapour diffuses out of the stomata more slowly when the air outside already holds a lot of water vapour.

options.text: Water evaporates from cells and diffuses out of stomata
options.rationale: In transpiration water evaporates from the cells inside the leaf and the water vapour diffuses out through the stomata, and the water lost is replaced by the transpiration stream in the xylem.

sectionTitle: Biology — Plant tissues, organs and systems
